competition: All-Russian Astronomy Olympiad — regional stage, grade 11

problems.problem: 1. Estimate at what distance a pole with a lamp can be so that at night it could be mistaken for a star near the horizon.

2. Two stars of solar mass revolve around their common centre of mass in 25 days. A third star, also similar to the Sun, revolves around this pair at a distance 100 times greater than the distance between the first two stars. What is the orbital period of the third star? Prove that this system is stable.

3. Two satellites fly around the Earth on the same orbit with eccentricity $e$ and semi-major axis $a$ and observe the Earth's surface. At the moment when one of them is at perigee, the other is at apogee. Determine what fraction of the Earth's surface they observe at this moment. Assume that even at perigee the distance of the satellite from the centre of the Earth is much greater than the radius of the Earth. Neglect atmospheric refraction.

4. The radiant of the Draconid meteor shower is located near the North pole of the ecliptic, and the meteors enter the Earth's atmosphere with a speed of 20 km/s. Determine the inclination of the orbit of the Draconids to the plane of the Earth's orbit.

5. A spacecraft of the future is moving away from the Earth with a speed of 3000 km/s. To maintain contact with the ship, every 1000 seconds a radio pulse is sent from the Earth to the ship, which exactly 1 second after its reception on the ship is sent back to the Earth. At what time interval will the return pulses be received on the Earth?
6. Two stars have the same masses and luminosities, but the surface of one of them is twice as hot as the surface of the other. Which of the stars has the greater mean density? By how many times?

1. The figure shows one of the constellations visible from the territory of our country. Name this constellation, label on the map handed out to you the names of stars you know, draw in and label the objects you know (galaxies, nebulae, star clusters). Label on the boundaries of the constellation the names of its neighbours on the celestial sphere. Can this constellation be seen today? If so, at what time of day?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/astronomy-olympiads-bank/main/images/rureg-2007-d1-q1-1.png

2. Barnard's Star has a proper motion of $10.3''$/year and a radial velocity of $-111$ km/s. When will it pass (or did it pass) at its minimum distance from the Sun, and what magnitude will it have then, if its parallax is $0.547''$ and its apparent magnitude is $9.53^m$?

3. On 4 February 1993 the demonstration space programme "Znamya-2" was successfully carried out, during which a large 20-metre flat thin-film mirror structure was deployed on board the cargo spacecraft "Progress M-15", and the experiment "New Light" on illuminating the night side of the Earth was carried out. Estimate what illuminance in "lunettes" (units of illuminance from the full Moon) can be created at the centre of the light spot on the Earth's surface, if it is known that the orbital altitude of the station was 350 km. Assume that the satellite is at the zenith and the solar rays fall on the ideal mirror at an angle of $50^\circ$ to its plane. The magnitudes of the Sun and the Moon are $-26.8^m$ and $-12.7^m$.

4. Why does the day of the vernal equinox not always fall on 21 March? When will the vernal equinox occur in 2081, if in 2004 it occurred at $06^\mathrm{h}49^\mathrm{m}$ Universal Time on 20 March? The length of the tropical year is 365.24219 days.

5. An artificial Earth satellite revolves around our planet on an elliptical orbit. At the perigee point its speed is equal to the second cosmic (escape) velocity for the apogee point. Find the eccentricity of the satellite's orbit.
6. Which stars are larger – blue supergiants or red supergiants? Why?

1. For an observer on the equator, the altitude of the Sun at the moment of the equinox is $30^\circ$, and its azimuth is $+90^\circ$. Determine the mean solar time at this point if the equation of time is $\eta = +7^\mathrm{m}$. Neglect refraction and the diurnal parallax of the Sun.

2. Determine the maximum angular distance between the radiant of a meteor shower and the beginning of the path of a meteor belonging to this shower, observed from the surface of the Earth. Assume that meteors light up in the atmosphere at an altitude of 100 km.
3. On a distant inhabited planet the thermal conditions are similar to those on Earth, but the local Sun has half the angular diameter. Find the temperature of this distant star.

4. A binary star consists of identical components, each of which is twice as massive as the Sun, moving on circular orbits around their common centre of mass. When observed from the Earth, the angular separation varies from $2''$ to $4''$ with a period of 10 years. Find the distance to the binary star.

5. The brightness of Venus at the moment of greatest elongation is $-4.5^m$ (phase 0.5, angular diameter $24''$), and that of Sirius is $-1.5^m$. Compare their surface brightness for an observer with a telescope of diameter 100 mm and magnification 100 times. Neglect the influence of the atmosphere; take the resolving power of the eye to be $1'$.

6. «And the stars, nevertheless, / and the stars, nevertheless, / are a little closer, but just as cold…» (the band "Zemlyane", "Grass by the House").

How in reality will the visual characteristics of stars change when observed from nearby outer space, if the distance and temperature are estimated from their apparent brightness and colour index?
1. Determine the duration of civil twilight for an observer on the equator and at the pole of the Earth. Neglect the apparent size of the Sun and atmospheric effects.

2. In which case is the duration of a central occultation of a star by the Moon (an occultation in which the star passes behind the centre of the lunar disc) longer – if the Moon is at perigee (apparent diameter $33.5'$) or at apogee (apparent diameter $29.5'$) of its orbit, and by how many times? Neglect the effects of the Earth's axial rotation.

3. In the Earth's sky there are 14 stars brighter than $1^m$, about 3 times more stars with brightness from $1^m$ to $2^m$, another 3 times more stars from $2^m$ to $3^m$, and so on. Can one believe an amateur astronomer who claimed that he saw Venus shining as brightly as all the stars of the night sky visible to the naked eye taken together?

4. The Moon, standing low above the horizon, is observed with a camera obscura – a dark room 4 metres long, in the wall of which a hole of diameter 1 cm is made, which serves as the objective of the camera. Estimate by how many times the illuminance of the image of the Moon in the camera obscura differs from that of the outer wall of the house illuminated by the Moon.
5. A red star is 2 times larger in diameter than its blue neighbour in a binary system. Which of the stars emits more energy? Estimate by how many times. Explain your answer.

6. In the tube of a refracting telescope with an objective diameter of 10 cm and a focal length of 1 m, a diaphragm is inserted at a distance of 10 cm from the objective; in the centre of the diaphragm there is a round hole of diameter 7 cm. What is the difference between the limiting magnitude at the centre of the field of view of such a telescope and the same quantity without the diaphragm in visual observations? What might such a diaphragm be needed for?

1. Write out all correct answers to each of the 4 questions:

1) Which constellations are not on modern star charts?
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Auriga} & \text{Boötes} & \text{Capricornus} & \text{Triangulum Minus} \\ \hline \text{Quadrans Muralis} & \text{Mensa} & \text{Sagittarius} & \text{Taurus} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

2) The radiants of which meteor showers are located in constellations not listed in question 1?
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline \alpha\text{-Aurigids} & \alpha\text{-Capricornids} & \text{Virginids} & \text{Geminids} \\ \hline \text{June Boötids} & \text{Quadrantids} & \text{Sagittarids} & \text{Taurids} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

3) Which objects are not part of the Solar System?
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Damocloids} & \text{Lacertids} & \text{Mirids} & \text{Monocerotids} \\ \hline \text{Perseids} & \text{Piscids} & \text{Ursids} & \text{Cepheids} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

4) Which objects are absent from our Galaxy?
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Achernar} & \text{Blazar} & \text{Quaoar} & \text{Quasar} \\ \hline \text{Magnetar} & \text{Mizar} & \text{Polar} & \text{Pulsar} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

2. The declination of star A is $60^\circ$, and the declination of star B is $30^\circ$. When photographed with a fixed camera with a CCD matrix and a long exposure, the stars look like short trails. The CCD counts in the trail corresponding to star A are twice as large as in the trail of star B. How are the magnitudes of these stars related? Neglect the field curvature of the camera, other aberrations and atmospheric absorption.

3. In 2009–2010 the system of rings and satellites of the planet Saturn will lie at a small angle to the direction from Saturn to the Sun. Estimate how many eclipses of Titan could be seen from Saturn in this period.

Known quantities: the radius of Saturn's orbit is 9.539 AU, the radius of Saturn is 60.25 thousand km, the mass of Saturn is 95.18 Earth masses, the radius of Titan's orbit is 1.222 million km. Titan's orbit lies in the plane of Saturn's equator; its inclination to the plane of Saturn's orbit is $25.3^\circ$. Consider all orbits to be circular; do not take into account the oblateness of Saturn and the shadow of its rings; neglect the size of Titan (consider an eclipse to be the immersion of the centre of Titan into the shadow of Saturn).

4. It is known that the star Aldebaran ($\alpha$ Tauri), a red giant with a mass of somewhat more than 2 solar masses, is seen in the sky among the stars of the open cluster Hyades, although it does not itself belong to this cluster. Which is closer to us – Aldebaran or the Hyades? Explain your answer.

5. What are the brightest objects that an observer could see in the sky whose eyes perceive only X-ray radiation? Describe two cases: the observer is on the surface of the Earth, and on an artificial Earth satellite.

6. Three spiral galaxies have similar characteristics and distances from the Earth. The disc of one of them is observed "face-on", the second at an angle of $45^\circ$ to the line of sight, the third "edge-on". For which of the three galaxies will it be possible to determine most accurately the relative mass contribution of "dark matter"?
1. How many sidereal days pass between two successive geocentric conjunctions of the Moon with some star near the ecliptic?

2. When observed from latitude $+55^\circ$, star A with declination $-2^\circ$ rose simultaneously with star B, and set simultaneously with star C. What is the difference of the right ascensions of stars B and C, if they are on the celestial equator? Neglect refraction.

3. During the period of smoke from forest fires in central Russia in summer 2010, an observer noticed that the Sun at an altitude of $20^\circ$ above the horizon had the same apparent brightness as the full Moon near the zenith has in a clear sky with a clean atmosphere. Based on this, estimate the total mass of smoke particles that were above one square metre of the Earth's surface in these regions. Assume that the absorption of light in the clean atmosphere at the zenith is $0.2^m$, and that the smoke consists of black particles of radius 1 μm and density 0.6 g/cm$^3$. Also assume that the absorption of light follows the laws of geometric optics (neglect diffraction on the particles).

4. A binary star consists of identical components of solar type revolving on a circular orbit around their common centre of mass. The system is an eclipsing variable, and every 5 years the hydrogen line H$\alpha$ (6563 Å) first splits by 1.0 Å and then merges again into one. What is the distance between the stars?
5. The angular diameter of the star Betelgeuse is $0.047''$, and its bolometric magnitude is $-2^m$. Find the effective temperature of Betelgeuse.

6. A cluster of galaxies has an apparent diameter of $1^\circ$ and consists of 1000 galaxies similar to our Galaxy. The redshift of the cluster is 0.1. Estimate how frequently collisions of galaxies will occur in this cluster.

1. The MiG-29M aircraft can reach a speed of up to 2500 km/h. By how many times is this greater (or less) than the speed of motion of the surface at the equator of a radio pulsar? than the orbital speed of the Dawn spacecraft revolving on a low circular orbit around the asteroid Vesta (mass $2.75\cdot10^{20}$ kg, radius 265 km)?

2. Mars, being at western quadrature, is observed in the constellation Sagittarius. In which constellation will it be during the following opposition? Assume that the orbit of Mars is circular and lies in the plane of the ecliptic; the orbit of the Earth is also circular.

3. Future inhabitants of the Earth decided to replace the Moon with a concave spherical mirror of the same diameter with a focal length equal to the radius of the Moon's orbit. What will the magnitude of such a "Moon" be when observed from the region of the Earth onto which the image of the Sun is focused? of Mars (at a mean opposition)? Assume that the axis of the mirror makes a small angle with the directions to the light source and to the Earth; neglect optical aberrations.
4. Astronomers discovered a new object – a nebula around a star, expanding with an angular speed of $0.2''$/day. Explain this phenomenon and find the distance to the object.

5. Future spaceship captains Kolya and Vasya were planning their journeys. Kolya said that he would quickly fly to $\alpha$ Centauri (G2V+K1V), from there to Altair ($\alpha$ Aquilae, A7V) and return to the Earth. To this Vasya replied that in the same time he would manage to visit Betelgeuse ($\alpha$ Orionis, M2Iab) and Rigel ($\beta$ Orionis, B8Ia) and return back. Which of them will complete his flight first, if the spaceships move with the same speed?

6. The binary star Porrima ($\gamma$ Virginis) consists of two identical components. The figure shows the measured positions of one of the stars (small crosses) relative to the other, which was considered fixed and is marked with a large cross. The measurements were made over the orbital period (169 years). The averaged positions are shown as the line of an ellipse. Assuming that the minor axis of the stars' orbits in space lies in the plane of the figure, find the inclination of the plane of the orbits itself to the plane of the figure.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/astronomy-olympiads-bank/main/images/rureg-2012-d1-q6-1.png
1. On 22 June at solar noon an observer standing upright on a level surface found that his shadow had a length equal to his height. At what latitude was the observer?
2. According to modern data, the mass fraction of oxygen in the Sun is 0.8%. For how many planetary atmospheres of the Earth type would the solar oxygen suffice?

3. Imagine that the Solar System has flown into a very dense homogeneous cloud of dark dust. As a result, the full Moon in the Earth's sky became fainter by $0.2^m$. List all celestial objects that will be visible in the Earth's sky to the naked eye. What (approximately) will their brightness be?

4. When observed from the Earth, the angular distance between a Galilean satellite of Jupiter and its shadow on the surface of the planet is equal to the apparent equatorial diameter of Jupiter. Which satellite is it? Consider the orbits of the Earth, Jupiter and the satellite to be circular.

5. Recently the mass media have been saying a lot that the red supergiant Betelgeuse ($\alpha$ Orionis) may at any moment explode, becoming a Supernova which in the Earth's sky will be comparable in brightness to the Sun. What will actually be the magnitude at the maximum of the outburst of Betelgeuse, if its explosion occurs in the near future? With which object in the sky will Betelgeuse be comparable in brightness at that time?

6. The figure shows the track of a planet of the Solar System (its position among the stars at different moments of time). The positions marked with circles are 10 days apart; dates are labelled every 30 days. Which planet is it?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/astronomy-olympiads-bank/main/images/rureg-2013-d1-q6-1.png

1. Two black holes coincide in their sizes (of the event horizon) with the Earth and the Moon and revolve around their common centre of mass on circular orbits 384 400 km apart from each other. What is the orbital period of such a system?

2. A receiver installed in the focal plane of a telescope registers optical radiation coming from a circular region of the sky of diameter $5''$. Which three celestial objects (not counting the Sun and objects on the Earth and in near-Earth orbit) will turn out to be the brightest for this receiver (in order of decreasing brightness)? Do not take into account non-stationary objects (bright comets, novae and supernovae).

3. A close conjunction of Venus and Mars is observed at some point of the Earth in the morning of 1 January at sunrise at an altitude of $46^\circ$ above the horizon. On what date will the nearest opposition of Mars occur? Consider the orbits of all the planets to be circular and lying in the plane of the ecliptic.

4. For his observations Christiaan Huygens used a refracting telescope with an objective diameter of 22 cm and a focal length of 64 m. The objective of this telescope was hung on a pole, and the observer with the eyepiece was on the ground. Suppose that, being at latitude $+52^\circ$, Huygens observed a celestial body with declination $+27^\circ$ at upper culmination. What distance does he need to walk during 15 minutes of observation in order to keep the body in the centre of the field of view all the time? Assume that Huygens used an eyepiece giving the equal-pupil magnification.

5. Two planets revolve on circular orbits around a distant star. One of them has an orbital period twice as long, and a spherical albedo half as large, as the other planet. At the same time, the mean temperature of the surfaces of both planets is the same. Find the spherical albedo of both planets. Do not take into account thermal effects from the interiors and atmospheres of the planets.
6. A certain elliptical galaxy has a brightness of $18^m$ and a redshift of 0.1. Estimate the mass of the galaxy. Neglect interstellar absorption.
1. The Sun and the Moon at the phase of first quarter set below the horizon simultaneously. At what latitude is the observer? Neglect refraction and the parallax of the Moon.
2. With what maximum angular speed among the stars can an artificial satellite in near-Earth orbit without engines move, when observed from the surface of our planet?

3. In images from the SOHO space observatory, stars down to $8^m$ are distinguishable at 20 angular radii of the Sun from its centre. What should the size of an asteroid be so that it could be detected near the Sun, at 20 radii from its centre in space? Consider the optical properties of the asteroid's surface to be similar to those of the Moon, the material to be refractory; neglect changes of properties due to heating.
4. A pulsar with a heliocentric period of 0.3 seconds has coordinates $\alpha = 18^\mathrm{h}$, $\delta = -55^\circ$. Within what limits will the observed period of this pulsar vary during a year?

5. What should the focal length of a ground-based telescope with an aperture of 20 cm be so that the amount of energy coming from Mars and from Antares ($1.1^m$) onto one pixel of a CCD matrix is the same? Assume that Mars is at a great opposition: its brightness is $-2.9^m$, its distance from the Earth is 56 million km. The size of a square pixel of the CCD matrix is 10 μm.

6. Before you is the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, on which stars are plotted according to their luminosity (or absolute magnitude in the V band) and colour index B–V (or effective temperature, if it is determined from this colour index). Suppose that a distant star, similar to the Sun and lying on the axis of the main sequence, has a fainter close companion, also located on the axis of the main sequence. The system is not resolved in a telescope, and the data of its photometry refer to the whole system. Draw a fragment of the diagram near the position of the Sun and mark where such a star can fall on it. Determine the maximum possible displacement of this star from the position of the main star in absolute magnitude and temperature. Consider the chemical composition of both stars of the system to be the same; neglect interstellar absorption of light.

1.

A star at the zenith had an apparent brightness of $0^\mathrm{m}$, and at an altitude of 30 degrees it became twice as faint. What magnitude will it have at an altitude of 20 degrees above the horizon? Consider the atmospheric conditions constant and uniform.

2.

Two bright stars, Sirius ($\alpha = 06^\mathrm{h}45.1^\mathrm{m}$, $\delta = -16^\circ43'$) and Vega ($\alpha = 18^\mathrm{h}36.9^\mathrm{m}$, $\delta = +38^\circ47'$), are located at the same altitude above the horizon. At what latitude on the Earth (to the nearest degree) will this altitude be the greatest?

3.

Long before an interplanetary station approaches Neptune from the direction of the Sun, the disk of its satellite Triton can be distinguished from the station with a certain telescope, and it looks the same (in apparent size and brightness) as Neptune itself does without a telescope. Find the diameter of the telescope's objective and its magnification. The geometric albedos of Neptune and Triton are 0.41 and 0.76 respectively.

4.

On the evening of 9 May 2016 a rare astronomical phenomenon will take place, a transit of Mercury across the disk of the Sun, which will be well visible in the European part of Russia. Determine how many times less often the May transits of Mercury occur than the November ones. Assume that during the May transits Mercury is at the aphelion of its orbit, and that the Earth's orbit is circular.

5.

According to one of the scientists' hypotheses, the role of dark matter particles may be played by "WIMPs" (WIMP – weakly interacting massive particle), elementary particles with an energy of about 100 GeV. Determine the average concentration of WIMPs in space, if the mass of the Galaxy within 50 kpc of the centre is estimated at $2\cdot10^{12}$ solar masses, and the fraction of dark matter in it is approximately 80%.

6.

The pulsar PSR B1257+12 was the first one around which a planet was found. The period of this pulsar is 6.22 ms, and its mass is 1.5 solar masses. The planet was discovered because the pulses were registered not at the times at which they should have arrived. The graph shows the dependence on time of the shift of the times of registration of the pulsar's pulses (compared with a model without this planet). Estimate the mass of the planet, assuming that the line of sight lies in the plane of its orbit.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/astronomy-olympiads-bank/main/images/rureg-2016-d1-q6-1.png

1.

A sundial consists of a vertical pole 4 m high and a flat horizontal dial. At some moment the shadow of the pole moved over the dial with an angular velocity of exactly 1 degree per minute. At what latitudes on the Earth could this have happened? What could the maximum length of the shadow be at that time? Neglect the angular size of the Sun. (O. S. Ugolnikov)

2.

A distant galaxy, similar to our Milky Way Galaxy, has a redshift of 0.01. At an angular distance of $5'$ from it its satellite, a dwarf galaxy, is seen. Estimate the period of its revolution around the large galaxy. (O. S. Ugolnikov)

3.

Scientists of the future proposed a fantastic project in which all the soil on the surface of Mars would be decomposed electrochemically into free metal and oxygen, and in this way an oxygen atmosphere would be created on the planet. What is the thickness of the soil layer that has to be processed so that the pressure of such an oxygen atmosphere at the surface of Mars is the same as the atmospheric pressure at the surface of the Earth? Assume that the soil of Mars consists of the mineral limonite with chemical formula $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$ and density $3.5\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$. The atomic weights of iron and oxygen are 56 and 16 respectively.

4.

The apparent magnitude of the star Regulus is $+1.4^\mathrm{m}$, its distance is 24 pc, its mass is 3.5 solar masses, and its axial rotation period is 16 hours. From these data, find the minimum possible value of the surface temperature of Regulus.

5.

In the Milky Way Galaxy, type II supernovae with absolute magnitude $-18^\mathrm{m}$ flare up once every 20 years. How often do such supernovae appear in the sky of the Earth brighter than Venus ($-4^\mathrm{m}$)? Take the radius of the Galaxy to be 15 kpc; the absorption of light is $2^\mathrm{m}$ per kpc. (O. S. Ugolnikov)

6.

The figure shows the dependence on time of the magnitude of a certain comet as seen from the Earth. Determine the semi-major axis and the eccentricity of the comet's orbit. Assume that the orbit lies in the plane of the ecliptic and does not go inside the Earth's orbit. The luminosity of the comet is inversely proportional to the fourth power of its distance from the Sun, and the comet scatters light uniformly in all directions. Consider the Earth's orbit circular. (O. S. Ugolnikov / E. N. Fadeev)

1.

A ground–space interferometer consists of two radio telescopes: one is installed on the surface of the Earth, the other on a satellite moving in orbit around the Earth. At the moment of observation the satellite was at a distance of 10 000 km from the centre of the Earth. For the ground antenna the satellite was at an altitude of $60^\circ$, and the source under study at an altitude of $30^\circ$, both at the same azimuth. Determine the resolution of the interferometer in this experiment if the observations were made at a wavelength of 18 cm. (E. N. Fadeev)

2.

At the pole of Jupiter's satellite Europa, on a high tower, a telescope was installed to study another satellite, Ganymede, and to map it. What part of the surface of Ganymede can be studied with this telescope? Consider the orbits of the satellites circular and lying in the plane of the equator of Jupiter and of the satellites themselves, and the sizes of the satellites much smaller than the radii of their orbits. Assume also that the whole disk of Ganymede is constantly above the horizon from the position of the telescope on the tower. (O. S. Ugolnikov)

3.

An optical star is part of a binary system with a dark compact object. The mass of the dark object is 1.4 solar masses. The motion around the centre of mass takes place in such a way that the optical star's annual parallactic displacement in the sky of the Earth disappears. Determine the mass of this star. Consider the orbits of the Earth and of the stars in the system circular.

4.

A star similar to the Sun revolves around the centre of the Galaxy. The velocity of the star relative to the Sun is 150 km/s. It is known that both stars are at the same distance from the centre of the Galaxy, equal to 8 kpc, and move in the same direction along a circle with the same speed of 220 km/s. Assuming that the mean interstellar absorption is $0.002^\mathrm{m}$/pc, find the apparent magnitude of this star. (S. V. Borisov)

5.

For a $12^\mathrm{m}$ star of spectral class G2V, brightness variations with a period of 10 years were discovered, caused by the transit of a planet across its disk: in the V band the depth was 1.500% in brightness, and in the H$\alpha$ line 1.520% in brightness. Estimate the size of the planet and the height of its atmosphere, assuming the atmosphere to consist of atomic hydrogen and to be opaque in the H$\alpha$ line, and the planet's orbit to be circular and lying along the line of sight. Determine the maximum angular distance between the planet and the star.

6.

The figure shows the spectrum of the galaxy SMM J2135-0102, which has a redshift $z = 2.33$. The abscissa shows the wavelength on a logarithmic scale, the ordinate the measured spectral flux density of the radiation, also on a logarithmic scale. This galaxy belongs to the so-called submillimetre galaxies: in them practically all the radiation of the stars is absorbed and re-emitted by dust in the submillimetre range of the electromagnetic spectrum. Estimate the characteristic temperature of the dust in the galaxy. (S. V. Pilipenko)

1.

At some place A, on the day of the vernal equinox, the Sun at upper culmination was twice as high as at place B, also at upper culmination, and its setting lasted one and a half times less than at place B. Find the latitudes of both places. Neglect refraction. (O. S. Ugolnikov)

2.

The beginning of the "Age of Aquarius" is sometimes defined as the moment when the vernal equinox point passes into the constellation Aquarius. This "Age" will begin in the year 2597. On what day at the present time does Mercury pass from the constellation Aquarius into the constellation Pisces, if at that moment it is at greatest western elongation and at the same time at the aphelion of its orbit? Consider the Earth's orbit circular, and Mercury's orbit lying in the plane of the ecliptic. (O. S. Ugolnikov)

3.

A large fixed radio telescope is installed at the centre of the far hemisphere of the Moon (selenographic coordinates $180^\circ$ longitude, $0^\circ$ latitude). The axis of the telescope points to the zenith, and the telescope can register objects no more than 2 degrees away from its axis. What part of the celestial sphere will be accessible to observations with this telescope if observations are made for 100 years? In the solution assume that the amplitude of the lunar librations in latitude is constant and equal to $6^\circ40'$. (O. S. Ugolnikov)

4.

Two trans-Neptunian objects are at distances of 50 and 100 AU from the Sun, and their albedos are 77% and 8% respectively. An infrared telescope operating in orbit around the Earth in a narrow spectral band at a wavelength of 100 μm recorded the same brightness for both bodies. Determine the difference of their magnitudes from the Earth in the optical range. (E. N. Fadeev)

5.

Another star of smaller mass flew past the Sun at a small distance. During the period of closest approach the heliocentric proper motion of the star was $1000''$ per year, and the wavelength of the H$\alpha$ line (6563 ångströms) in its spectrum increased by 0.010 ångström in one year. Find the minimum distance between the Sun and the star. (O. S. Ugolnikov)

6.

A binary system consists of identical components similar to the Sun. The graph shows the dependence on time of the angular distance between them (in arcseconds) in the sky of the Earth. Determine the eccentricity of the orbit, the inclination of the orbital plane to the line of sight and the distance to the system. (O. S. Ugolnikov)

1.

6. A very scary problem

In 2007 the first fast radio burst, FRB 010724, was discovered. Figure 1 shows the record of the burst signal from the Parkes telescope (Australia) in 96 frequency channels at intervals of 1 ms. The equatorial coordinates of the burst source are $\alpha = 01^\mathrm{h}18^\mathrm{m}06^\mathrm{s}$, $\delta = -75^\circ12'19''$.

It is known that radio waves undergo dispersion when propagating in a plasma. The propagation speed of long waves in a plasma is smaller than that of short ones. The difference in the arrival times of the signal at frequencies $\nu_1$ and $\nu_2$ is

$$t_2 - t_1 = \frac{e^2}{2\pi m_\mathrm{e} c}\left(\frac{1}{\nu_2^2} - \frac{1}{\nu_1^2}\right) DM,$$

where $e$ and $m_\mathrm{e}$ are the charge and mass of the electron, and $DM$ is the dispersion measure:

$$DM\ [\mathrm{pc/cm^3}] = \bar{n}_\mathrm{e}\, d,$$

where $\bar{n}_\mathrm{e}$ is the mean electron concentration along the line of sight and $d$ is the distance to the source.

In astronomy it is customary to use the Gaussian system of units, in which mass is expressed in grams, time in seconds and length in centimetres. In these units the electron charge is $e = 4.8\cdot10^{-10}\ \mathrm{g^{1/2}\,cm^{3/2}\,s^{-1}}$, and the dispersion measure has the dimension $\mathrm{cm^{-2}}$. However, the dispersion measure is usually expressed in $\mathrm{pc/cm^3}$.

A. Find the dispersion measure $DM$ of FRB 010724 in $\mathrm{pc/cm^3}$.

B. Assuming that the electron concentration along the line of sight is constant and equal to the mean value for the disk of the Galaxy, $n = 3\cdot10^{-2}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, find the distance to the burst source.

C. Do you think the distance you obtained is overestimated or underestimated? Explain your answer.

10. A supernova problem

A record-fast decrease of the dispersion measure DM has been found for a source of repeating fast radio bursts. It is believed that this is related to the expansion of a supernova remnant and, thereby, to the decrease of the density of this remnant.

It may be assumed that the supernova remnant is fully ionised and is at the stage of free expansion. Then the change of the dispersion measure with time due to the expansion of the remnant can be expressed as

$$DM = 260\ \mathrm{pc/cm^3}\left(\frac{M}{10M_\odot}\right)^{2}\times\left(\frac{E_0}{10^{44}\ \mathrm{J}}\right)^{-1}\times\left(\frac{t}{100\ \text{yr}}\right)^{-2},$$

where $M$ is the mass of the ejecta, $E_0$ is the energy of the explosion, and $t$ is the time elapsed since the explosion. The measurements of the dispersion measure for this source are shown in the figure.

A. Determine from the graph the rate of change of the dispersion measure.

B. Determine the age of the supernova remnant in years.

C. Determine the expansion speed of the supernova envelope, assuming it constant. Take $E_0 = 2\cdot10^{44}$ J.

D. Determine the present radius of the remnant in parsecs.

The graph shows data relating only to the supernova remnant; all other factors contributing to the observed value of DM have been subtracted.

The figure shows the evolution of the dispersion measure over about 3 years of observations, starting from some moment in the recent past. The abscissa shows continuous time counts in days. The ordinate shows the dispersion measure DM. The horizontal bold line marks the mean value of the dispersion measure over the interval shown. A dashed line is also drawn on the graph, corresponding to the best linear model for determining the rate of decrease of DM over this time interval.

For reference. The dispersion measure DM is a characteristic of the medium through which the radiation passes, determining the different arrival times of signals at the observer at different frequencies. The dispersion measure is equal to the total number of electrons along the line of sight in a column of cross-section 1 cm$^2$ and is measured in astronomy in units of pc/cm$^3$:

$$DM\ [\mathrm{pc/cm^3}] = \langle n_\mathrm{e}\rangle\, r,$$

where $\langle n_\mathrm{e}\rangle$ is the mean electron concentration along the line of sight and $r$ is the distance to the source.
